      "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "Conclusion\nWe suggest KG-GPT, a versatile framework that\nutilizes LLMs for tasks that use KGs. KG-GPT is\ndivided into three stages: Sentence Segmentation,\nGraph Retrieval, and Inference, each designed for\nbreaking down sentences, sourcing related graph\nelements, and reaching reasoned outcomes, respec-\ntively. We assess KG-GPT’s efficacy using KG-\nbased fact verification and KGQA metrics, and\nthe model demonstrates consistent, impressive re-\nsults, even surpassing a number of fully-supervised\nmodels. Consequently, our research signifies a sub-\nstantial advancement in combining structured and\nunstructured data management in the LLMs’ con-\ntext.\n",

      "quote": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "Conclusion\nIn this work, we introduce a new GraphQA benchmark for real-world graph question answering and\npresent G-Retriever, an architecture adept at complex and creative queries. Experimental results show\nthat G-Retriever surpasses baselines in textual graph tasks across multiple domains, scales effectively\nwith larger graph sizes, and demonstrates resistance to hallucination.\n9\n\nLimitations and Future Work: Currently, G-Retriever employs a static retrieval component. Future\ndevelopments could investigate more sophisticated RAG where the retrieval is trainable.\n",

      "quote": "Conclusion\nWe suggest KG-GPT, a versatile framework that\nutilizes LLMs for tasks that use KGs. KG-GPT is\ndivided into three stages: Sentence Segmentation,\nGraph Retrieval, and Inference, each designed for\nbreaking down sentences, sourcing related graph\nelements, and reaching reasoned outcomes, respec-\ntively. We assess KG-GPT’s efficacy using KG-\nbased fact verification and KGQA metrics, and\nthe model demonstrates consistent, impressive re-\nsults, even surpassing a number of fully-supervised\nmodels. Consequently, our research signifies a sub-\nstantial advancement in combining structured and\nunstructured data management in the LLMs’ con-\ntext.\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n",

      "quote": "Recently, many techniques have been explored to improve the reasoning ability of LLMs by plan-\nning, which first prompts LLMs to generate a reasoning plan and then conduct reasoning based on it\n(Wang et al., 2023c). However, LLMs are known for having hallucination issues, which are prone to\ngenerating incorrect plans and leading to wrong answers (Ji et al., 2023). To address this issue, we\npresent a novel planning-retrieval-reasoning framework, which makes the reasoning plans grounded\nby KGs and then retrieves faithful reasoning paths for LLM reasoning.\nRelation paths, which capture semantic relations between entities, have been utilized in many rea-\nsoning tasks on KGs (Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022). Moreover, compared to the dynamically\nupdated entities, the relations in KGs are more stable (Wang et al., 2023a). By using relation paths,\nwe can always retrieve the latest knowledge from KGs for reasoning. Therefore, relation paths can\nserve as faithful plans for reasoning the answer to KGQA task.\nExample 2. Given a question “Who is the child of Alice”, we can generate a relation path as the\nplan: z = marry to →father of. This relation path expresses the plan: 1) find the person that\n“Alice” is married to; 2) find the child of that person. We can execute the plan (relation path) by\nretrieving a reasoning path from KGs as: wz = Alice\nmarry to\n−−−−−−→Bob\nfather of\n−−−−−−→Charlie. Finally,\nwe can answer the question based on the reasoning path, which is “Charlie”.\n",

      "quote": "Knowledge Graphs (KGs) (Pan et al., 2017b,a)\nusually store accurate knowledge in a structured\nway. We find that a KG pattern can be viewed as\nthe abstract of a complex question, as shown in\nFigure 1, which reveals the connection between\nquestion planning and patterns. This opens up\nthe possibility of constructing training data to en-\nhance the planning capabilities of LLMs using KGs.\nSpecifically, we start by grounding predefined pat-\nterns in an open-domain KG to extract numerous\ninstances, which we then verbalize into complex\nquestions and corresponding sub-questions in nat-\nural language. In this way, we effectively create\na large number of accurate planning data for fine-\ntuning. Being fine-tuned with these planning data,\nLLMs’ capability of generating plans for complex\nquestions is enhanced, resulting in better final an-\nswers by parsing and executing these plans. We\nrefer to this innovative framework as Learning to\nPlan from Knowledge Graphs (LPKG).\n",

      "quote": "A.6\nIMPLEMENTATION SETTINGS\nFor RoG, we use LLaMA2-Chat-7B (Touvron et al., 2023) as the LLM backbone, which is instruc-\ntion finetuned on the training split of WebQSP and CWQ as well as Freebase for 3 epochs. The\nbatch size is set to 4 and the learning rate is set to 2e-5. We use the cosine learning rate scheduler\npolicy with the warmup ratio set to 0.03. The training is conducted on 2 A100-80G GPUs for 38\nhours. During inference, we first adopt the LLM to generate top-K relation paths with the highest\nprobability as the plans. Then, we adopt the Algorithm 1 to retrieve reasoning paths, which are fed\ninto the LLM to reason the final answers.\nFor LLM beelines, we use zero-shot prompting to conduct KGQA, which directly asks LLMs to\nanswer the question.       "quote": "By treating relation paths as plans, we can make sure the plans are grounded by KGs, which enables\nLLMs to conduct faithful and interpretable reasoning on graphs. In a nutshell, we formulate our\nRoG as an optimization problem that aims to maximize the probability of reasoning the answer from\na knowledge graph G w.r.t the question q by generating relation paths z as the plan:\nPθ(a|q, G) =\nX\nz∈Z\nPθ(a|q, z, G)Pθ(z|q),\n(1)\nwhere θ denotes the parameters of LLMs, z denotes the relation paths (plans) generated by LLMs,\nand Z denotes the set of possible relation paths. The latter term Pθ(z|q) is the probability of gen-\nerating a faithful relation path z grounded by KG, given the question q, which is realized by the\nplanning module. The former term Pθ(a|q, z, G) is the probability of reasoning an answer a given\nthe question q, relation path z, and KG G, which is computed by the retrieval-reasoning module.\n4.2\nOPTIMIZATION FRAMEWORK\nDespite the advantage of generating relation paths as plans, the LLMs have zero knowledge of the\nrelations contained in KGs. Therefore, LLMs cannot directly generate relation paths grounded by\nKGs as faithful plans. Moreover, LLMs might not understand the reasoning paths correctly and\nconduct reasoning based on them. To address these issues, we design two instruction tuning tasks:\n1) planning optimization, which distills the knowledge from KGs into LLMs to generate faithful\nrelation paths as plans; 2) retrieval-reasoning optimization, which enables LLMs to reason based on\nthe retrieved reasoning paths.\n",

      "quote": "By treating relation paths as plans, we can make sure the plans are grounded by KGs, which enables\nLLMs to conduct faithful and interpretable reasoning on graphs. In a nutshell, we formulate our\nRoG as an optimization problem that aims to maximize the probability of reasoning the answer from\na knowledge graph G w.r.t the question q by generating relation paths z as the plan:\nPθ(a|q, G) =\nX\nz∈Z\nPθ(a|q, z, G)Pθ(z|q),\n(1)\nwhere θ denotes the parameters of LLMs, z denotes the relation paths (plans) generated by LLMs,\nand Z denotes the set of possible relation paths. The latter term Pθ(z|q) is the probability of gen-\nerating a faithful relation path z grounded by KG, given the question q, which is realized by the\nplanning module. The former term Pθ(a|q, z, G) is the probability of reasoning an answer a given\nthe question q, relation path z, and KG G, which is computed by the retrieval-reasoning module.\n4.2\nOPTIMIZATION FRAMEWORK\nDespite the advantage of generating relation paths as plans, the LLMs have zero knowledge of the\nrelations contained in KGs. Therefore, LLMs cannot directly generate relation paths grounded by\nKGs as faithful plans. Moreover, LLMs might not understand the reasoning paths correctly and\nconduct reasoning based on them. To address these issues, we design two instruction tuning tasks:\n1) planning optimization, which distills the knowledge from KGs into LLMs to generate faithful\nrelation paths as plans; 2) retrieval-reasoning optimization, which enables LLMs to reason based on\nthe retrieved reasoning paths.\n",

      "title": "Learning to Plan for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models from Knowledge Graphs",
      "page_start": 2,

      "source_spans": [

      ],
      "quote": "Knowledge Graphs (KGs) (Pan et al., 2017b,a)\nusually store accurate knowledge in a structured\nway. We find that a KG pattern can be viewed as\nthe abstract of a complex question, as shown in\nFigure 1, which reveals the connection between\nquestion planning and patterns. This opens up\nthe possibility of constructing training data to en-\nhance the planning capabilities of LLMs using KGs.\nSpecifically, we start by grounding predefined pat-\nterns in an open-domain KG to extract numerous\ninstances, which we then verbalize into complex\nquestions and corresponding sub-questions in nat-\nural language. In this way, we effectively create\na large number of accurate planning data for fine-\ntuning. Being fine-tuned with these planning data,\nLLMs’ capability of generating plans for complex\nquestions is enhanced, resulting in better final an-\nswers by parsing and executing these plans. We\nrefer to this innovative framework as Learning to\nPlan from Knowledge Graphs (LPKG).\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have achieved\nsignificant success in open-domain question an-\nswering. However, they continue to face chal-\nlenges such as hallucinations and knowledge\ncutoffs. These issues can be mitigated through\nin-context learning by providing LLMs with\nrelevant context before generating answers.\nRecent literature proposes Knowledge Graph\nPrompting (KGP) which integrates knowledge\ngraphs with an LLM-based traversal agent\nto substantially enhance document retrieval\nquality. However, KGP requires costly fine-\ntuning with large datasets and remains prone\nto hallucination. In this paper, we propose\nCuriousLLM, an enhancement that integrates\na curiosity-driven reasoning mechanism into\nan LLM agent. This mechanism enables the\nagent to generate relevant follow-up questions,\nthereby guiding the information retrieval pro-\ncess more efficiently. Central to our approach\nis the development of the new Follow-upQA\ndataset, which includes questions and support-\ning evidence as input, with follow-up ques-\ntions serving as ground truths. These follow-\nup questions either inquire about what is still\nmissing to fully answer the user’s query or\nuse special tokens to signify that the retrieved\nevidence is sufficient. Our experiments show\nthat CuriousLLM significantly boosts LLM per-\nformance in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), circumventing the substantial\ncomputational costs and latency from the orig-\ninal KGP framework. Source code: https:\n//github.com/zukangy/KGP-CuriousLLM.\n1\n",

To implement the interface-augmented\napproach, there remain two key problems, namely\nhow to design suitable interfaces for specific tasks\nand how to utilize them for reasoning by LLMs,\nwhich are the focus of this work.\nTo design suitable interfaces, we regard multi-\nple types of structured data as black-box systems,\nand design the interfaces to provide accurate, effi-\ncient data access and filtering for LLMs. For each\narXiv:2305.09645v2  [cs.CL]  23 Oct 2023\n\ninterface, its implementation is dependent on the\ncharacteristic of the structured data, while its func-\ntionality is general to all LLMs, with just a few\narguments for specifying the data requirements.\nBased on these interfaces, we propose an Itera-\ntive Reading-then-Reasoning (IRR) framework for\nLLMs to utilize the interfaces to solve the tasks\nbased on structured data, namely StructGPT. This\nframework considers two major functions to ful-\nfill different tasks, namely collecting relevant evi-\ndence (reading) and inferring the answer or plan-\nning subsequent steps (reasoning). Specifically, we\npropose an invoking-linearization-generation pro-\ncedure to support LLMs in reading and reasoning\non the structured data with the help of the external\ninterfaces.       "quote": "To this end, we propose a new general frame-\nwork, called KG-GPT, that uses LLMs’ reasoning\ncapabilities to perform KG-based tasks. KG-GPT\nis similar to StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023) in that\nboth reason on structured data using LLMs. How-\never, unlike StructGPT which identifies paths from\na seed entity to the final answer entity within KGs,\nKG-GPT retrieves the entire sub-graph and then\ninfers the answer. This means KG-GPT can be\nused not only for KGQA but also for tasks like\nKG-based fact verification.\nKG-GPT consists of three steps: 1) Sentence\n(Claim / Question) Segmentation, 2) Graph Re-\ntrieval, and 3) Inference. During Sentence Seg-\nmentation, a sentence is partitioned into discrete\nsub-sentences, each aligned with a single triple (i.e.\n[head, relation, tail]). The subsequent step, namely\nGraph Retrieval, retrieves a potential pool of rela-\ntions that could bridge the entities identified within\nthe sub-sentences. Then, a candidate pool of evi-\ndence graphs (i.e. sub-KG) is obtained using the\nretrieved relations and the entity set. In the final\nstep, the obtained graphs are used to derive a logi-\ncal conclusion, such as validating a given claim or\nanswering a given question.\nTo evaluate KG-GPT, we employ KG-based\nfact verification and KGQA benchmarks, both de-\nmanding complex reasoning that utilizes structured\nknowledge of KGs. In KG-based fact verification,\nwe use FACTKG (Kim et al., 2023), which includes\narXiv:2310.11220v1  [cs.CL]  17 Oct 2023\n",

      "quote": "1. Additionally, this technique tends to exhaust its\npreset search budget because it lacks a mechanism\nto determine when to stop the search, even when\nthe retrieved documents are sufficient to answer the\nquestion. The more passages supplied to the LLM\nfor response generation, the higher the latency of\nthe QA system, since the LLM must reason through\n1\narXiv:2404.09077v3  [cs.CL]  18 Feb 2025\n\nFigure 1: Two common types of questions in HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018): (1) Comparison questions require\nparallel reasoning over different documents. (2) Bridging questions require sequential reasoning.\nall passages to arrive at an answer.\nTo address these challenges, we propose a novel\nframework by fine-tuning an LLM agent to emulate\nthe curious nature of a human researcher. Instead of\npredicting missing evidence, our agent asks follow-\nup questions to more efficiently guide the search\ntoward missing evidence. Compared to the orig-\ninal approach, our CuriousLLM: 1) requires sig-\nnificantly fewer training samples for fine-tuning,\n2) markedly improves MD-QA performance, and\n3) can terminate the search before exhausting the\npreset search budget, thereby reducing latency. Our\ncontributions are as follows.\n• Follow-upQA Dataset: We introduce a new\ndataset specifically designed to train LLMs\nto generate pertinent follow-up questions that\nenhance the retrieval process within the KGP\nframework for MD-QA tasks. In addition, we\noffer this dataset as a benchmark to inspire\nfurther research.\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nIn this paper, we aim to improve the reason-\ning ability of large language models (LLMs)\nover structured data in a unified way.\nIn-\nspired by the studies on tool augmentation for\nLLMs, we develop an Iterative Reading-then-\nReasoning (IRR) framework to solve question\nanswering tasks based on structured data, called\nStructGPT. In this framework, we construct\nthe specialized interfaces to collect relevant ev-\nidence from structured data (i.e., reading), and\nlet LLMs concentrate on the reasoning task\nbased on the collected information (i.e., rea-\nsoning). Specially, we propose an invoking-\nlinearization-generation procedure to support\nLLMs in reasoning on the structured data with\nthe help of the interfaces. By iterating this\nprocedure with provided interfaces, our ap-\nproach can gradually approach the target an-\nswers to a given query. Experiments conducted\non three types of structured data show that\nStructGPT greatly improves the performance\nof LLMs, under the few-shot and zero-shot set-\ntings. Our codes and data are publicly available\nat https://github.com/RUCAIBox/StructGPT.\n1\n",

In this way, LLMs can concentrate on\nreasoning based on the evidence obtained from the\ninterfaces. To implement the interface-augmented\napproach, there remain two key problems, namely\nhow to design suitable interfaces for specific tasks\nand how to utilize them for reasoning by LLMs,\nwhich are the focus of this work.\nTo design suitable interfaces, we regard multi-\nple types of structured data as black-box systems,\nand design the interfaces to provide accurate, effi-\ncient data access and filtering for LLMs. For each\narXiv:2305.09645v2  [cs.CL]  23 Oct 2023\n\ninterface, its implementation is dependent on the\ncharacteristic of the structured data, while its func-\ntionality is general to all LLMs, with just a few\narguments for specifying the data requirements.\nBased on these interfaces, we propose an Itera-\ntive Reading-then-Reasoning (IRR) framework for\nLLMs to utilize the interfaces to solve the tasks\nbased on structured data, namely StructGPT. This\nframework considers two major functions to ful-\nfill different tasks, namely collecting relevant evi-\ndence (reading) and inferring the answer or plan-\nning subsequent steps (reasoning). Specifically, we\npropose an invoking-linearization-generation pro-\ncedure to support LLMs in reading and reasoning\non the structured data with the help of the external\ninterfaces. By iterating this procedure with pro-\nvided interfaces, we can gradually approach the\ntarget answer to a given question.\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have achieved\nsignificant success in open-domain question an-\nswering. However, they continue to face chal-\nlenges such as hallucinations and knowledge\ncutoffs. These issues can be mitigated through\nin-context learning by providing LLMs with\nrelevant context before generating answers.\nRecent literature proposes Knowledge Graph\nPrompting (KGP) which integrates knowledge\ngraphs with an LLM-based traversal agent\nto substantially enhance document retrieval\nquality. However, KGP requires costly fine-\ntuning with large datasets and remains prone\nto hallucination. In this paper, we propose\nCuriousLLM, an enhancement that integrates\na curiosity-driven reasoning mechanism into\nan LLM agent. This mechanism enables the\nagent to generate relevant follow-up questions,\nthereby guiding the information retrieval pro-\ncess more efficiently. Central to our approach\nis the development of the new Follow-upQA\ndataset, which includes questions and support-\ning evidence as input, with follow-up ques-\ntions serving as ground truths. These follow-\nup questions either inquire about what is still\nmissing to fully answer the user’s query or\nuse special tokens to signify that the retrieved\nevidence is sufficient. Our experiments show\nthat CuriousLLM significantly boosts LLM per-\nformance in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), circumventing the substantial\ncomputational costs and latency from the orig-\ninal KGP framework. Source code: https:\n//github.com/zukangy/KGP-CuriousLLM.\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nIn this paper, we aim to improve the reason-\ning ability of large language models (LLMs)\nover structured data in a unified way.\nIn-\nspired by the studies on tool augmentation for\nLLMs, we develop an Iterative Reading-then-\nReasoning (IRR) framework to solve question\nanswering tasks based on structured data, called\nStructGPT. In this framework, we construct\nthe specialized interfaces to collect relevant ev-\nidence from structured data (i.e., reading), and\nlet LLMs concentrate on the reasoning task\nbased on the collected information (i.e., rea-\nsoning). Specially, we propose an invoking-\nlinearization-generation procedure to support\nLLMs in reasoning on the structured data with\nthe help of the interfaces. By iterating this\nprocedure with provided interfaces, our ap-\nproach can gradually approach the target an-\nswers to a given query. Experiments conducted\non three types of structured data show that\nStructGPT greatly improves the performance\nof LLMs, under the few-shot and zero-shot set-\ntings. Our codes and data are publicly available\nat https://github.com/RUCAIBox/StructGPT.\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nThe ‘pre-train, prompt, predict’ paradigm of large language\nmodels (LLMs) has achieved remarkable success in open-\ndomain question answering (OD-QA). However, few works\nexplore this paradigm in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), a task demanding a thorough understanding\nof the logical associations among the contents and structures\nof documents. To fill this crucial gap, we propose a Knowl-\nedge Graph Prompting (KGP) method to formulate the right\ncontext in prompting LLMs for MD-QA, which consists of\na graph construction module and a graph traversal module.\nFor graph construction, we create a knowledge graph (KG)\nover multiple documents with nodes symbolizing passages or\ndocument structures (e.g., pages/tables), and edges denoting\nthe semantic/lexical similarity between passages or document\nstructural relations. For graph traversal, we design an LLM-\nbased graph traversal agent that navigates across nodes and\ngathers supporting passages assisting LLMs in MD-QA. The\nconstructed graph serves as the global ruler that regulates the\ntransitional space among passages and reduces retrieval la-\ntency. Concurrently, the graph traversal agent acts as a local\nnavigator that gathers pertinent context to progressively ap-\nproach the question and guarantee retrieval quality. Extensive\nexperiments underscore the efficacy of KGP for MD-QA, sig-\nnifying the potential of leveraging graphs in enhancing the\nprompt design and retrieval augmented generation for LLMs.\nOur code: https://github.com/YuWVandy/KG-LLM-MDQA.\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nAnswering real-world complex queries, such as complex product search, often\nrequires accurate retrieval from semi-structured knowledge bases that involve blend\nof unstructured (e.g., textual descriptions of products) and structured (e.g., en-\ntity relations of products) information. However, many previous works studied\ntextual and relational retrieval tasks as separate topics. To address the gap, we\ndevelop STARK, a large-scale Semi-structure retrieval benchmark on Textual\nand Relational Knowledge Bases. Our benchmark covers three domains: product\nsearch, academic paper search, and queries in precision medicine. We design a\nnovel pipeline to synthesize realistic user queries that integrate diverse relational\ninformation and complex textual properties, together with their ground-truth an-\nswers (items). We conduct rigorous human evaluation to validate the quality of\nour synthesized queries. We further enhance the benchmark with high-quality\nhuman-generated queries to provide an authentic reference. STARK serves as a\ncomprehensive testbed for evaluating the performance of retrieval systems driven\nby large language models (LLMs). Our experiments suggest that STARK presents\nsignificant challenges to the current retrieval and LLM systems, highlighting the\nneed for more capable semi-structured retrieval systems.\n[\n]\nAnswer:\nQuery\nSemi-structured KB (SKB)\n…\nUser\nRetrieve\nEvaluate\nSTARK\nPlease suggest a HEAD \ntennis racquet for casual\nplayer?\n[\n]\nLooking for stylish kids \nbike helmets that suit a \nSuperman bike.\n…\nConstruct with\nsimulated users\n…\nCan you find a\npush-along tricycle \nfrom Radio Flyer that is\nboth fun and safe for \nmy kids?\n…\nLLM Retrieval system\n[\n]\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have achieved\nsignificant success in open-domain question an-\nswering. However, they continue to face chal-\nlenges such as hallucinations and knowledge\ncutoffs. These issues can be mitigated through\nin-context learning by providing LLMs with\nrelevant context before generating answers.\nRecent literature proposes Knowledge Graph\nPrompting (KGP) which integrates knowledge\ngraphs with an LLM-based traversal agent\nto substantially enhance document retrieval\nquality. However, KGP requires costly fine-\ntuning with large datasets and remains prone\nto hallucination. In this paper, we propose\nCuriousLLM, an enhancement that integrates\na curiosity-driven reasoning mechanism into\nan LLM agent. This mechanism enables the\nagent to generate relevant follow-up questions,\nthereby guiding the information retrieval pro-\ncess more efficiently. Central to our approach\nis the development of the new Follow-upQA\ndataset, which includes questions and support-\ning evidence as input, with follow-up ques-\ntions serving as ground truths. These follow-\nup questions either inquire about what is still\nmissing to fully answer the user’s query or\nuse special tokens to signify that the retrieved\nevidence is sufficient. Our experiments show\nthat CuriousLLM significantly boosts LLM per-\nformance in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), circumventing the substantial\ncomputational costs and latency from the orig-\ninal KGP framework. Source code: https:\n//github.com/zukangy/KGP-CuriousLLM.\n1\n",

      "quote": "5.1\nPerformance Comparison on MD-QA\nWe compare the MD-QA performance of the proposed\nKGP-T5 and other baselines in Table 1. Firstly, the base-\nlines ‘None/Golden’ achieve the worst/best performance be-\ncause one provides no context and the other provides the\ngolden context. Our proposed methods\nKGP-T5 rank at the Top-1 except for the Golden baseline.\nThe 2nd-performing baseline MDR fine-tunes a RoBERTa-\nbase encoder by predicting the next supporting fact based\non the question and the already retrieved contexts (Xiong\net al. 2020). This next-passage prediction pretext task equips\nthe model with the reasoning capability of the knowledge\nacross different passages and hence increases the quality\nof the retrieved contexts. The other deep-learning-based re-\ntriever DPR achieves much worse performance than MDR\nbecause it only fine-tunes the encoder by maximizing the\nsimilarity between the query and its supporting facts regard-\nless of their sequential order, demonstrating the importance\nof understanding the logical order of different knowledge\nwhen solving MD-QA (Xiong et al. 2020).       "quote": "Figure 2: Demonstration of Semi-structured Knowledge Bases, where each knowledge base combines\nboth textual and relational information in a complex way, making the retrieval tasks challenging.\n• Context-specific reasoning: The queries entail reasoning capabilities specific to the context. This\nincludes the ability to infer customer interests, understand specialized field descriptions, and deduce\nrelationships involving multiple subjects mentioned within the query. For example, the context “I\nhad a dozen 2.5-inch Brybelly air hockey pucks, so I’m trying to find matching strikers.” entails the\nuser’s interest in looking for complementary products.       "quote": "5.4\nSensitivity Analysis\nHere we perform the sensitivity analysis of the branching\nfactor (the number of nodes selected from candidate neigh-\nbors to visit next). However, as\nwe fix the context budget to ensure fair comparison (i.e., the\ntotal number of passages we are allowed to retrieve for each\nquestion is the same across all baselines), the performance\ndeclines as the branching factor increases because the num-\nber of initial seeding nodes diminishes, leading to reduced\ncoverage of the KG.       "quote": "Abstract\nThe ‘pre-train, prompt, predict’ paradigm of large language\nmodels (LLMs) has achieved remarkable success in open-\ndomain question answering (OD-QA). However, few works\nexplore this paradigm in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), a task demanding a thorough understanding\nof the logical associations among the contents and structures\nof documents. To fill this crucial gap, we propose a Knowl-\nedge Graph Prompting (KGP) method to formulate the right\ncontext in prompting LLMs for MD-QA, which consists of\na graph construction module and a graph traversal module.\nFor graph construction, we create a knowledge graph (KG)\nover multiple documents with nodes symbolizing passages or\ndocument structures (e.g., pages/tables), and edges denoting\nthe semantic/lexical similarity between passages or document\nstructural relations. For graph traversal, we design an LLM-\nbased graph traversal agent that navigates across nodes and\ngathers supporting passages assisting LLMs in MD-QA. The\nconstructed graph serves as the global ruler that regulates the\ntransitional space among passages and reduces retrieval la-\ntency. Concurrently, the graph traversal agent acts as a local\nnavigator that gathers pertinent context to progressively ap-\nproach the question and guarantee retrieval quality. Extensive\nexperiments underscore the efficacy of KGP for MD-QA, sig-\nnifying the potential of leveraging graphs in enhancing the\nprompt design and retrieval augmented generation for LLMs.\nOur code: https://github.com/YuWVandy/KG-LLM-MDQA.\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nAnswering real-world complex queries, such as complex product search, often\nrequires accurate retrieval from semi-structured knowledge bases that involve blend\nof unstructured (e.g., textual descriptions of products) and structured (e.g., en-\ntity relations of products) information. However, many previous works studied\ntextual and relational retrieval tasks as separate topics. To address the gap, we\ndevelop STARK, a large-scale Semi-structure retrieval benchmark on Textual\nand Relational Knowledge Bases. Our benchmark covers three domains: product\nsearch, academic paper search, and queries in precision medicine. We design a\nnovel pipeline to synthesize realistic user queries that integrate diverse relational\ninformation and complex textual properties, together with their ground-truth an-\nswers (items). We conduct rigorous human evaluation to validate the quality of\nour synthesized queries. We further enhance the benchmark with high-quality\nhuman-generated queries to provide an authentic reference. STARK serves as a\ncomprehensive testbed for evaluating the performance of retrieval systems driven\nby large language models (LLMs). Our experiments suggest that STARK presents\nsignificant challenges to the current retrieval and LLM systems, highlighting the\nneed for more capable semi-structured retrieval systems.\n[\n]\nAnswer:\nQuery\nSemi-structured KB (SKB)\n…\nUser\nRetrieve\nEvaluate\nSTARK\nPlease suggest a HEAD \ntennis racquet for casual\nplayer?\n[\n]\nLooking for stylish kids \nbike helmets that suit a \nSuperman bike.\n…\nConstruct with\nsimulated users\n…\nCan you find a\npush-along tricycle \nfrom Radio Flyer that is\nboth fun and safe for \nmy kids?\n…\nLLM Retrieval system\n[\n]\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have achieved\nsignificant success in open-domain question an-\nswering. However, they continue to face chal-\nlenges such as hallucinations and knowledge\ncutoffs. These issues can be mitigated through\nin-context learning by providing LLMs with\nrelevant context before generating answers.\nRecent literature proposes Knowledge Graph\nPrompting (KGP) which integrates knowledge\ngraphs with an LLM-based traversal agent\nto substantially enhance document retrieval\nquality. However, KGP requires costly fine-\ntuning with large datasets and remains prone\nto hallucination. In this paper, we propose\nCuriousLLM, an enhancement that integrates\na curiosity-driven reasoning mechanism into\nan LLM agent. This mechanism enables the\nagent to generate relevant follow-up questions,\nthereby guiding the information retrieval pro-\ncess more efficiently. Central to our approach\nis the development of the new Follow-upQA\ndataset, which includes questions and support-\ning evidence as input, with follow-up ques-\ntions serving as ground truths. These follow-\nup questions either inquire about what is still\nmissing to fully answer the user’s query or\nuse special tokens to signify that the retrieved\nevidence is sufficient. Our experiments show\nthat CuriousLLM significantly boosts LLM per-\nformance in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), circumventing the substantial\ncomputational costs and latency from the orig-\ninal KGP framework. Source code: https:\n//github.com/zukangy/KGP-CuriousLLM.\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "Figure 4 in Appendix F illustrates MindMap’s per-\nformance on diverse question types.\nFor drug-\nrelated questions (a) and (d), which demand in-\ndepth knowledge, MindMap outperforms other\nmethods.\nDisease-related questions (b) and (f)\nshow comparable results between retrieval methods\nand MindMap, indicating that incorporating exter-\nnal knowledge mitigates errors in language model\noutputs. Notably, for general knowledge questions\n(c), LLMs like GPT-3.5 perform better, while re-\ntrieval methods lag.       "quote": "• KG retrieval + GPT-3.5 We compare with exist-\ning KG retrieval methods (Jia et al., 2021; Sun\net al., 2023), which aim to find the shortest KG\npath between every pair of question entities. TOT is a method that uses\na tree structure to solve complex problems(Yao\net al., 2023a). By extending one inference path\ninto multiple inference paths, the model can syn-\nthesize the results of multiple inference paths to\nobtain the final conclusion.\nD\nPrompt Engine\n• The instructions of MindMap components.\nTable 9 shows the instruction of Step I: en-\ntity recognition, which aims to identify and\nlabel medical entities in the user query.       "quote": "ToG starts from each of the N entities/relations (nodes/edges on knowledge graph) and searches\nall its neighboring relations/entities.       "quote": "From the default state, Tree-of-Traversals can\neither Think, Answer, or choose to ExpandKG.\nAfter Tree-of-Traversals chooses to ExpandKG,\nit first is prompted to Select_Entities\nabout which it needs more information (e.g.,\n‘Inception’ in Figure 1).\nIt is then prompted\nto Select_Relation from a list of candi-\ndate relations provided by the KG interface’s\nget_relations method. After selecting a re-\nlation (e.g., ‘cast member’ in Figure 1), all edges\ncontaining one of the selected entities as the source\nand the selected relation as the relation are added to\nthe local KG subgraph. Tree-of-Traversals is then\nable to Answer, Think, or ExpandKG again.\nPrompt Templates.\nEach state in the ASM other\nthan the ‘done’ state is associated with a unique\nprompt template. Prompt templates are filled with\ninformation from the local KG subgraph and the\nKG interface before presenting them to the LLM.\nA customized prompt for each state allows us to\npresent precise and relevant information along with\nspecific instructions for each state to the LLM sim-\nplifying the LLM’s task. For instance, the prompt\nfor ‘selecting-entities’ presents the available op-\ntions of entities to choose from that are in the local\nKG subgraph (see Figure 3). Prompt templates for\nall the states are in the Appendix F.1-F.3.\nLocal KG subgraph is represented using a a to-\nken efficient YAML format that minimizes repeti-\ntion for multiple edges on the same entity.\n",

      "quote": "3. Development of a new dataset to test com-\nbined reasoning over a general and a domain-\nspecific KG, and evaluation of Tree-of-\nTraversals on this dataset.\nWe conduct detailed experiments on three mod-\nels of varied sizes hosted on Amazon Bedrock and\npresent detailed ablation studies.\n2\nTree-of-Traversals\nThe Tree-of-Traversals algorithm maintains a local\nKG subgraph that is repeatedly expanded until it\ncontains all the information required by an LLM\nto answer the given query. At the start, a local\nKG subgraph is initialized to contain the entities\npresent in the original query. It is then expanded\nusing a tree search algorithm to choose actions and\nthoughts generated by an LLM in order to obtain\nrelevant knowledge from the KG using a KG inter-\nface. The algorithm halts when the LLM is able\nto answer the original query using the local KG\nsubgraph as context. Tree-of-Traversals consists of\nthree major components. (1) A knowledge graph\ninterface implemented to interact with one or more\nrequired KGs. (2) An action state machine (ASM)\nwhich is a finite state machine that defines the fea-\nsible space of actions, states, and prompt templates\nwhen the LLM interacts with a KG to expand the\nlocal KG subgraph. (3) A tree search algorithm\nwhich defines the overall LLM search trajectory\nsuch as best first search, backtrack upon making a\nmistake, and termination condition when an answer\nis found.\n2.1\nKnowledge Graph Interface\n",

      "quote": "Difference with Naive Beam Search\nToG is slightly\ndifferent from the beam search. ToG uses the top-N rea-\nsoning paths as evidence while the naive beam search\nchooses the most plausible path as the only reasoning path.\nWe conduct naive top1-beam search methods for ToG on\nCWQ and WebQSP. For each depth of the ToG, we choose\nthe reasoning path with the highest plausibility, to evaluate\nif the current reasoning path is sufficient to answer the\nquestions. The experiment results are shown in Table 6. In\nnaive beam search, the calibration error accumulates along\n17\n\nPublished as a conference paper at ICLR 2024\nFigure 5: Exemplar sensitivity analysis for CWQ and WebQSP for ToG, where \"0\" denotes zero-shot\nand \"k\" denotes k-shot.\nFigure 6: The erroneous instances and categories in the CWQ, WebQSP, and GrailQA of IO, CoT,\nand ToG.\nthe inference, leading to the instability of the final result.\nWe believe that ToG can partially alleviate this issue by\nconsidering the top-N reasoning paths.\n",

      "quote": "From the default state, Tree-of-Traversals can\neither Think, Answer, or choose to ExpandKG.\nAfter Tree-of-Traversals chooses to ExpandKG,\nit first is prompted to Select_Entities\nabout which it needs more information (e.g.,\n‘Inception’ in Figure 1).\nIt is then prompted\nto Select_Relation from a list of candi-\ndate relations provided by the KG interface’s\nget_relations method. After selecting a re-\nlation (e.g., ‘cast member’ in Figure 1), all edges\ncontaining one of the selected entities as the source\nand the selected relation as the relation are added to\nthe local KG subgraph. Tree-of-Traversals is then\nable to Answer, Think, or ExpandKG again.\nPrompt Templates.\nEach state in the ASM other\nthan the ‘done’ state is associated with a unique\nprompt template. Prompt templates are filled with\ninformation from the local KG subgraph and the\nKG interface before presenting them to the LLM.\nA customized prompt for each state allows us to\npresent precise and relevant information along with\nspecific instructions for each state to the LLM sim-\nplifying the LLM’s task. For instance, the prompt\nfor ‘selecting-entities’ presents the available op-\ntions of entities to choose from that are in the local\nKG subgraph (see Figure 3). Prompt templates for\nall the states are in the Appendix F.1-F.3.\nLocal KG subgraph is represented using a a to-\nken efficient YAML format that minimizes repeti-\ntion for multiple edges on the same entity.\n",

      ],
      "quote": "TF-IDF KG Construction\nFor adding edges according to\nlexical similarity, we first apply TF-IDF keyword extrac-\ntion (Ramos et al. 2003) over each document to filter out\nmeaningless words such as supporting verbs and articles,\nwhich also reduces the dimension of bag-of-word (BOW)\nfeatures, sparsifies the constructed graph and increases the\ngraph traversal efficiency. In addition, we add the document\ntitle into the extracted keyword set since some questions fo-\ncus on title entities. We collect the extracted keywords from\nall documents to form the keyword space W and then con-\nnect two passages if they share any common keyword in W.\nKNN-ST/MDR KG Construction\nFor adding edges ac-\ncording to semantic similarity, we can readily employ pre-\nexisting models such as sentence transformers to gener-\nate passage embedding Xi for each node vi and subse-\nquently compute pairwise similarity matrix to construct the\nK-nearest neighbor (KNN) graph. However, these off-the-\nshelf models, typically trained on tasks not so-related to\nMD-QA, may not adequately encapsulate necessary logical\nassociations in their embedding similarity demanded by the\nquestion. To overcome this problem, we follow the train-\ning strategy of MDR (Xiong et al. 2020) and train a sen-\ntence encoder by predicting the subsequent supporting facts\nbased on previously supporting facts, thereby endowing the\nencoder with reasoning capability. Consequently, the em-\nbedding similarity and the corresponding constructed KNN\ngraph fundamentally encapsulate the necessary logical asso-\nciations between different passages.\n",

      "quote": "To verify the constructed KGs indeed encode the neces-\nsary information for MD-QA, we randomly sample ques-\ntions from HotpotQA and construct KGs over the set of\ndocuments for each of these questions using our proposed\nmethods. We vary the hyperparameters to control the spar-\nsity of the constructed KG and measure how much percent-\nage of the supporting facts are covered by neighbors of the\nseeding passages initially searched by TF-IDF. More details\nabout the four construction methods and their hyperparame-\nters are included in Section 8.5 in Supplementary. As shown\nin Figure 5, as the constructed graph becomes denser, the\nchance that the neighboring node passages hit the support-\ning facts increases (i.e., SF-EM increases) although the re-\ndundant information also increases (i.e., the precision de-\ncreases). Given the common keywords shared between one\npassage to all other passages are typically far less than the\ntotal number of passages across all documents, the density of\nthe constructed graph by TF-IDF would be upper-bounded,\ncausing lower SF-EM (evidenced by SF-EM below 0.7 in\nFigure 5 for TF-IDF curve). For TAGME, we empirically\nfind it identifies a larger quantity of entities mentioned in\na single passage, which leads to a denser graph and causes\nthe starting SF-EM of TAGME to be already around 0.95.\nIn addition, since KNN-MDR is pre-trained by predicting\nthe next supporting facts (Xiong et al. 2020) on HotpotQA,\nit achieves better trade-off than KNN-ST where the embed-\ndings are directly obtained from the sentence transformer\nwithout dataset-specific pre-training.\n",

      "quote": "Despite numerous well-established KGs (Hoffart et al. 2013;\nTian et al. 2023b), they treat nodes/edges as entities/rela-\ntions, which necessitates sophisticated relational extraction\ntechniques and thereby limits their applicability in general\ndomains (Huang et al. 2021). Additionally, their primary fo-\ncus on the Wikipedia domain also restricts their usage for\nanswering non-Wikipedia questions such as ones over legal\nor financial documents. To remedy this issue, we propose\ngenerally applicable KG construction methods.\nWe first analyze two representative questions in Fig-\nure 2(a)-(b) to motivate our KG construction. Answering\nthese two questions necessitates the deduction of logical as-\nsociations among different passages. These associations are\nencoded either through 1) lexical similarity: common key-\nwords shared among different passages, e.g., ‘Alf Clausen’\nbridges passage S1 and passage S2 in Figure 2(a), or 2) se-\nmantic similarity: syntactic elements that convey semantic\nrelations, e.g., ‘nationality’ and ‘American director’ in Fig-\nure 2(b). This motivates us to construct the graph by mod-\neling passages as nodes and their lexical/semantic similarity\nas edges. More specifically in Figure 3, we split each docu-\nment into individual passages, and for each passage Si, we\nadd a node vi to the KG with its feature being the text of that\npassage Xi. Then we add edges by checking the lexical/se-\nmantic similarity between pairs of passage nodes.\n",

      ],
      "quote": "TF-IDF KG Construction\nFor adding edges according to\nlexical similarity, we first apply TF-IDF keyword extrac-\ntion (Ramos et al. 2003) over each document to filter out\nmeaningless words such as supporting verbs and articles,\nwhich also reduces the dimension of bag-of-word (BOW)\nfeatures, sparsifies the constructed graph and increases the\ngraph traversal efficiency. In addition, we add the document\ntitle into the extracted keyword set since some questions fo-\ncus on title entities. We collect the extracted keywords from\nall documents to form the keyword space W and then con-\nnect two passages if they share any common keyword in W.\nKNN-ST/MDR KG Construction\nFor adding edges ac-\ncording to semantic similarity, we can readily employ pre-\nexisting models such as sentence transformers to gener-\nate passage embedding Xi for each node vi and subse-\nquently compute pairwise similarity matrix to construct the\nK-nearest neighbor (KNN) graph. However, these off-the-\nshelf models, typically trained on tasks not so-related to\nMD-QA, may not adequately encapsulate necessary logical\nassociations in their embedding similarity demanded by the\nquestion. To overcome this problem, we follow the train-\ning strategy of MDR (Xiong et al. 2020) and train a sen-\ntence encoder by predicting the subsequent supporting facts\nbased on previously supporting facts, thereby endowing the\nencoder with reasoning capability. Consequently, the em-\nbedding similarity and the corresponding constructed KNN\ngraph fundamentally encapsulate the necessary logical asso-\nciations between different passages.\n",

      "quote": "To verify the constructed KGs indeed encode the neces-\nsary information for MD-QA, we randomly sample ques-\ntions from HotpotQA and construct KGs over the set of\ndocuments for each of these questions using our proposed\nmethods. We vary the hyperparameters to control the spar-\nsity of the constructed KG and measure how much percent-\nage of the supporting facts are covered by neighbors of the\nseeding passages initially searched by TF-IDF. More details\nabout the four construction methods and their hyperparame-\nters are included in Section 8.5 in Supplementary. As shown\nin Figure 5, as the constructed graph becomes denser, the\nchance that the neighboring node passages hit the support-\ning facts increases (i.e., SF-EM increases) although the re-\ndundant information also increases (i.e., the precision de-\ncreases). Given the common keywords shared between one\npassage to all other passages are typically far less than the\ntotal number of passages across all documents, the density of\nthe constructed graph by TF-IDF would be upper-bounded,\ncausing lower SF-EM (evidenced by SF-EM below 0.7 in\nFigure 5 for TF-IDF curve). For TAGME, we empirically\nfind it identifies a larger quantity of entities mentioned in\na single passage, which leads to a denser graph and causes\nthe starting SF-EM of TAGME to be already around 0.95.\nIn addition, since KNN-MDR is pre-trained by predicting\nthe next supporting facts (Xiong et al. 2020) on HotpotQA,\nit achieves better trade-off than KNN-ST where the embed-\ndings are directly obtained from the sentence transformer\nwithout dataset-specific pre-training.\n",

      "quote": "B.1\nMANUAL ANALYSIS (CONTINUE)\nThe manual analysis results presented in Table 5 reveal several additional observations:\n1) Even though ToG-2 consistently outperforms the baselines across various datasets, it still faces\nsignificant bottlenecks when it comes to information retrieval. For instance, Wikidata often\ncontains inaccuracies, contradictions, or gaps, and many Wiki entities are missing key details on\ntheir Wikipedia pages.       "quote": "The advantage of ToG-2 can be summarized as: (1) In-depth retrieval: ToG-2 achieves in-depth\nand reliable context retrieval through the guide of KGs and performs precise graph retrieval by\ntreating documents as node contexts, achieving a tight-coupling combination of KG and text RAG,\nenabling deep and comprehensive retrieval processes. (2) Faithful reasoning: ToG-2 iteratively\nperforms a collaborative retrieval process based on KG and text, using retrieved heterogeneous\nknowledge as the basis for LLM reasoning and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM-generated con-\ntent (3) Efficiency and Effectiveness: a) ToG-2 is a training-free and plug-and-play framework that\ncan be applied to various LLMs; b) ToG-2 can be executed between any associated KG and docu-\nment database, while for purely document database, entities can be extracted from the documents\nfirst, and then a graph can be constructed through relation extraction or entity co-occurrence (Edge\net al., 2024); c) ToG-2 achieves new SOTA performances on various complex knowledge reasoning\ndatasets and can elevate the reasoning capabilities of smaller LLMs, e.g., Llama2-13B to a level\ncomparable to direct reasoning with powerful LLMs like GPT-3.5.\n2\n",

      "quote": "B.2\nSUPPLEMENTARY ANALYSIS FOR THE MAIN RESULTS\nAs we observed a performance discrepancy between ToG and ToG-2 on the Creak dataset in Table 1,\nwe aim to provide a more detailed analysis on this particular dataset. We include all of the prompts and the LLMs versions in the above steps in Appendix E.\n2.5\nSynthesized Data Distribution Analysis and Human Evaluation\n• Query and Answer Length.       "quote": "B.1\nMANUAL ANALYSIS (CONTINUE)\nThe manual analysis results presented in Table 5 reveal several additional observations:\n1) Even though ToG-2 consistently outperforms the baselines across various datasets, it still faces\nsignificant bottlenecks when it comes to information retrieval. These issues are largely due to in-\ncomplete knowledge sources and the limitations of retrieval models. For instance, Wikidata often\ncontains inaccuracies, contradictions, or gaps, and many Wiki entities are missing key details on\ntheir Wikipedia pages. On the retrieval side, different types of questions require different informa-\ntion, and a one-size-fits-all retrieval model can struggle without specific training. Therefore, ToG-2\ncan be further optimized through plug-ins that incorporate more comprehensive knowledge graphs\nand more advanced retrieval models, which is convenient.\n2) When handling less straightforward or more complex questions, LLMs can sometimes misun-\nderstand the intent. For example, in the question “What number president nominated Annie Caputo\nto become a member of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission?” the correct answer is 45th but the\nmodel might answer Donald Trump (which, while true, isn’t exactly what the question was asking).\n",

      "quote": "The advantage of ToG-2 can be summarized as: (1) In-depth retrieval: ToG-2 achieves in-depth\nand reliable context retrieval through the guide of KGs and performs precise graph retrieval by\ntreating documents as node contexts, achieving a tight-coupling combination of KG and text RAG,\nenabling deep and comprehensive retrieval processes. (2) Faithful reasoning: ToG-2 iteratively\nperforms a collaborative retrieval process based on KG and text, using retrieved heterogeneous\nknowledge as the basis for LLM reasoning and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM-generated con-\ntent (3) Efficiency and Effectiveness: a) ToG-2 is a training-free and plug-and-play framework that\ncan be applied to various LLMs; b) ToG-2 can be executed between any associated KG and docu-\nment database, while for purely document database, entities can be extracted from the documents\nfirst, and then a graph can be constructed through relation extraction or entity co-occurrence (Edge\net al., 2024); c) ToG-2 achieves new SOTA performances on various complex knowledge reasoning\ndatasets and can elevate the reasoning capabilities of smaller LLMs, e.g., Llama2-13B to a level\ncomparable to direct reasoning with powerful LLMs like GPT-3.5.\n2\n",

      "quote": "Results\nWe present our retrieval and QA experimental results below. Given that our method indirectly affects\nQA performance, we report QA results on our best-performing retrieval backbone ColBERTv2 [70].\nHowever, we report retrieval results for several strong single-step and multi-step retrieval techniques.\nSingle-Step Retrieval Results. As seen in Table 2, HippoRAG outperforms all other methods,\nincluding recent LLM-augmented baselines such as Propositionizer and RAPTOR, on our main\ndatasets, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, while achieving competitive performance on HotpotQA.\nWe notice an impressive improvement of 11 and 20% for R@2 and R@5 on 2WikiMultiHopQA\nand around 3% on MuSiQue. This difference can be partially explained by 2WikiMultiHopQA’s\nentity-centric design, which is particularly well-suited for HippoRAG. Our lower performance on\nHotpotQA is mainly due to its lower knowledge integration requirements, as explained in Appendix\nB, as well as a due to a concept-context tradeoff which we alleviate with an ensembling technique\ndescribed in Appendix F.2.\nMulti-Step Retrieval Results. For multi-step or iterative retrieval, our experiments in Table 3\ndemonstrate that IRCoT [78] and HippoRAG are complementary. Using HippoRAG as the re-\ntriever for IRCoT continues to bring R@5 improvements of around 4% for MuSiQue, 18% for\n2WikiMultiHopQA and an additional 1% on HotpotQA.\n6\n\nTable 4: QA performance. HippoRAG’s QA improvements correlate with its retrieval improvements\non single-step (rows 1-3) and multi-step retrieval (rows 4-5).\nMuSiQue\n2Wiki\nHotpotQA\nAverage\nRetriever\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\nEM\nF1\n",

      "quote": "The findings on MetaQA are presented in Table 2.\nThe performance of KG-GPT is impressive, scoring\n96.3%, 94.4%, and 94.0% on 1-hop, 2-hop, and 3-\nhop tasks respectively. This demonstrates its strong\nability to generalize from a limited number of ex-\namples, a critical trait when handling real-world\napplications with varying degrees of complexity.\nStage\nFactKG\nMetaQA\nMetaQA\nMetaQA\n1-hop\n2-hop\n3-hop\nSentence\n39\n3\n63\n100\nSegmentation\nGraph Retrieval\n17\n4\n3\n0\nInference\n44\n93\n34\n0\nTable 3: Number of errors from 100 incorrect samples\nacross each dataset.\nInterestingly, the performance of KG-GPT\nclosely matches that of a fully-supervised model.\nParticularly, it surpasses KV-Mem by margins of\n0.1%, 11.7%, and 45.1% across three distinct tasks\nrespectively, signifying its superior performance.\nWhile the overall performance of KG-GPT is simi-\nlar to that of GraftNet, a noteworthy difference is\npronounced in the 3-hop task, wherein KG-GPT\noutperforms GraftNet by 16.3%.       "quote": "PPR Alternatives. As shown in Table 5 (rows 5-6), to examine how much of our results are due to\nthe strength of PPR, we replace the PPR output with the query node probability #»n multiplied by node\nspecificity values (row 5) and a version of this that also distributes a small amount of probability to the\ndirect neighbors of each query node (row 6). First, we find that PPR is a much more effective method\nfor including associations for retrieval on all three datasets compared to both simple baselines. It is\ninteresting to note that adding the neighborhood of Rq nodes without PPR leads to worse performance\nthan only using the query nodes themselves.\nAblations. As seen in Table 5 (rows 7-8), node specificity obtains considerable improvements on\nMuSiQue and HotpotQA and yields almost no change in 2WikiMultiHopQA. This is likely because\n2WikiMultiHopQA relies on named entities with little differences in terms of term weighting. In\ncontrast, synonymy edges have the largest effect on 2WikiMultiHopQA, suggesting that noisy entity\nstandardization is useful when most relevant concepts are named entities, and improvements to\nsynonymy detection could lead to stronger performance in other datasets.\n5.2\nHippoRAG’s Advantage: Single-Step Multi-Hop Retrieval\n",

As seen in Table 2, HippoRAG outperforms all other methods,\nincluding recent LLM-augmented baselines such as Propositionizer and RAPTOR, on our main\ndatasets, MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, while achieving competitive performance on HotpotQA.\nWe notice an impressive improvement of 11 and 20% for R@2 and R@5 on 2WikiMultiHopQA\nand around 3% on MuSiQue. This difference can be partially explained by 2WikiMultiHopQA’s\nentity-centric design, which is particularly well-suited for HippoRAG. Our lower performance on\nHotpotQA is mainly due to its lower knowledge integration requirements, as explained in Appendix\nB, as well as a due to a concept-context tradeoff which we alleviate with an ensembling technique\ndescribed in Appendix F.2.\nMulti-Step Retrieval Results. For multi-step or iterative retrieval, our experiments in Table 3\ndemonstrate that IRCoT [78] and HippoRAG are complementary. Using HippoRAG as the re-\ntriever for IRCoT continues to bring R@5 improvements of around 4% for MuSiQue, 18% for\n2WikiMultiHopQA and an additional 1% on HotpotQA.\n6\n\nTable 4: QA performance.       "quote": "Abstract\nIn this paper, we aim to improve the reason-\ning ability of large language models (LLMs)\nover structured data in a unified way.\nIn-\nspired by the studies on tool augmentation for\nLLMs, we develop an Iterative Reading-then-\nReasoning (IRR) framework to solve question\nanswering tasks based on structured data, called\nStructGPT. In this framework, we construct\nthe specialized interfaces to collect relevant ev-\nidence from structured data (i.e., reading), and\nlet LLMs concentrate on the reasoning task\nbased on the collected information (i.e., rea-\nsoning). Specially, we propose an invoking-\nlinearization-generation procedure to support\nLLMs in reasoning on the structured data with\nthe help of the interfaces. By iterating this\nprocedure with provided interfaces, our ap-\nproach can gradually approach the target an-\nswers to a given query. Experiments conducted\non three types of structured data show that\nStructGPT greatly improves the performance\nof LLMs, under the few-shot and zero-shot set-\ntings. Our codes and data are publicly available\nat https://github.com/RUCAIBox/StructGPT.\n1\n",

      "page_start": 1,

      "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nIn this paper, we aim to improve the reason-\ning ability of large language models (LLMs)\nover structured data in a unified way.\nIn-\nspired by the studies on tool augmentation for\nLLMs, we develop an Iterative Reading-then-\nReasoning (IRR) framework to solve question\nanswering tasks based on structured data, called\nStructGPT. In this framework, we construct\nthe specialized interfaces to collect relevant ev-\nidence from structured data (i.e., reading), and\nlet LLMs concentrate on the reasoning task\nbased on the collected information (i.e., rea-\nsoning). Specially, we propose an invoking-\nlinearization-generation procedure to support\nLLMs in reasoning on the structured data with\nthe help of the interfaces. By iterating this\nprocedure with provided interfaces, our ap-\nproach can gradually approach the target an-\nswers to a given query. Experiments conducted\non three types of structured data show that\nStructGPT greatly improves the performance\nof LLMs, under the few-shot and zero-shot set-\ntings.       "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3.       "quote": "8. Even though ToG-2 integrates additional knowl-\nedge through entity context, ToG-2 still manages to\n9\n\nPublished as a conference paper at ICLR 2025\nreduce the entity pruning phase to 68.7% of ToG’s runtime on average. This is because ToG relies\non LLM-based entity pruning, while ToG-2 leverages DRMs, which can handle more candidates\nand compute relevance scores faster.\n4.7\nMANUAL ANALYSIS\nTo what extent does ToG-2 leverage the triple links and the contextual information? To gain a\ndeeper understanding of ToG-2’s behavior, we randomly select 50 AdvHotpotQA reasoning results\nfrom ToG-2 and perform a manual analysis about how triple link reasoning and the contextual in-\nformation of entities within the links contribute to the correct answers, respectively. As shown in\nTable 4, Doc-enhanced Answers have the highest proportion, at approximately 42%, while Triple-\nenhanced Answers are the least common, indicating that textual context is often the most important\nsource of information for complex QA tasks. Triple links alone lack detailed context, making it\ndifficult to provide deeper insights, and their role is more of a macro-level guide. Even without\nrelying on the text information within the triples, key clues can still be navigated effectively. The\nproportion of Both-enhanced Answer shows significant utilization, suggesting that the combination\nof triple-link reasoning and entity context documents is a highly effective pattern. Direct Answers\naccount for 16% of the responses, showing that for complex questions, the LLM can directly answer\nrelatively few questions and still relies heavily on advanced information-enhanced pipelines.\n",

      "quote": "Considering the aforementioned challenges, we propose Think-on-Graph 2.0 (ToG-2), a tight-\ncoupling hybrid (KG×Text) RAG paradigm which effectively integrates unstructured knowledge\nfrom texts with structured insights from KGs, serving as a roadmap to enhance complex problem-\nsolving. As shown in Figure 1(d), ToG-2 first initializes the starting point for graph search by\nextracting topic entities from the question. At the beginning of each retrieval round, ToG-2 explores\nmore candidate entities by performing relation retrieval on the KG and retrieves relevant text from\ndocuments associated with these candidate entities. Following knowledge-guided context retrieval,\nToG-2 prunes the candidate entities based on the results of the context retrieval, updates the set of\ntopic entities and uses it as the starting point for the next round of retrieval. After each retrieval\nround, ToG-2 prompts the LLM to answer the question based on the highly relevant knowledge\ntriples and contexts obtained during the retrieval process. If the retrieved information is insufficient\nto answer the question, the next round of retrieval continues for searching more in-depth clues. Such\na tight-coupling hybrid RAG paradigm makes LLM perform closer to human when solving complex\n2\n\nPublished as a conference paper at ICLR 2025\nproblems: examining current clues and associating potential entities based on their existing knowl-\nedge framework, continuously digging into the topic until finding the answer.\n",

      "quote": "B.2\nSUPPLEMENTARY ANALYSIS FOR THE MAIN RESULTS\nAs we observed a performance discrepancy between ToG and ToG-2 on the Creak dataset in Table 1,\nwe aim to provide a more detailed analysis on this particular dataset. This analysis will offer insights\ninto the underlying factors contributing to the observed discrepancy. Furthermore, we will showcase\nand discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the strengths and limitations of\nboth methods in the context of the Creak dataset. Specifically, we manually analyzed the reasoning\nprocess for 50 examples. As a result, ToG already performs well on this dataset, and the richer entity\ndocument information utilized by ToG-2 does not provide significant additional benefits. As shown\nin the table, ToG-2 produces a higher proportion of Triple-enhanced Answers on Creak compared\nto more complex datasets like HotpotQA.\nWe conducted a detailed case study of the behavior of ToG and ToG-2, highlighting three represen-\ntative cases that elucidate the primary reasons for the observed performance differences.
