      "quote": "ABSTRACT\nAlthough large language models (LLMs) have achieved significant success in vari-\nous tasks, they often struggle with hallucination problems, especially in scenarios\nrequiring deep and responsible reasoning. These issues could be partially addressed\nby introducing external knowledge graphs (KG) in LLM reasoning. In this paper,\nwe propose a new LLM-KG integrating paradigm “LLM ⊗KG” which treats the\nLLM as an agent to interactively explore related entities and relations on KGs\nand perform reasoning based on the retrieved knowledge. We further implement\nthis paradigm by introducing a new approach called Think-on-Graph (ToG), in\nwhich the LLM agent iteratively executes beam search on KG, discovers the most\npromising reasoning paths, and returns the most likely reasoning results. We use\na number of well-designed experiments to examine and illustrate the following\nadvantages of ToG: 1) compared with LLMs, ToG has better deep reasoning power;\n2) ToG has the ability of knowledge traceability and knowledge correctability by\nleveraging LLMs reasoning and expert feedback; 3) ToG provides a flexible plug-\nand-play framework for different LLMs, KGs and prompting strategies without\nany additional training cost; 4) the performance of ToG with small LLM models\ncould exceed large LLM such as GPT-4 in certain scenarios and this reduces the\ncost of LLM deployment and application. As a training-free method with lower\ncomputational cost and better generality, ToG achieves overall SOTA in 6 out of\n9 datasets where most previous SOTAs rely on additional training. Our code is\npublicly available at https://github.com/IDEA-FinAI/ToG.\n1\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nIn this paper, we aim to improve the reason-\ning ability of large language models (LLMs)\nover structured data in a unified way.\nIn-\nspired by the studies on tool augmentation for\nLLMs, we develop an Iterative Reading-then-\nReasoning (IRR) framework to solve question\nanswering tasks based on structured data, called\nStructGPT. In this framework, we construct\nthe specialized interfaces to collect relevant ev-\nidence from structured data (i.e., reading), and\nlet LLMs concentrate on the reasoning task\nbased on the collected information (i.e., rea-\nsoning). Specially, we propose an invoking-\nlinearization-generation procedure to support\nLLMs in reasoning on the structured data with\nthe help of the interfaces. By iterating this\nprocedure with provided interfaces, our ap-\nproach can gradually approach the target an-\nswers to a given query. Experiments conducted\non three types of structured data show that\nStructGPT greatly improves the performance\nof LLMs, under the few-shot and zero-shot set-\ntings. Our codes and data are publicly available\nat https://github.com/RUCAIBox/StructGPT.\n1\n",

      "quote": "CoT\n46.0\n67.3\nToG-R\n67.6\n81.9\nToG\n69.5\n82.6\nGain\n(+23.5)\n(+15.3)\nTable 2: Performances of ToG using different back-\nbone models on CWQ and WebQSP.\nGiven the plug-and-play convenience of ToG,\nwe try three LLMs in experiments: ChatGPT,\nGPT-4 and Llama-2. We use OpenAI API to call\nChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) and GPT-41. Llama-\n2-70B-Chat (Touvron et al., 2023) runs with 8\nA100-40G without quantization, where the tem-\nperature parameter is set to 0.4 for exploration\nprocess (increasing diversity) and set to 0 for rea-\nsoning process (guaranteeing reproducibility).\nThe maximum token length for the generation\nis set to 256.       "quote": "Abstract\nIn this paper, we aim to improve the reason-\ning ability of large language models (LLMs)\nover structured data in a unified way.\nIn-\nspired by the studies on tool augmentation for\nLLMs, we develop an Iterative Reading-then-\nReasoning (IRR) framework to solve question\nanswering tasks based on structured data, called\nStructGPT. In this framework, we construct\nthe specialized interfaces to collect relevant ev-\nidence from structured data (i.e., reading), and\nlet LLMs concentrate on the reasoning task\nbased on the collected information (i.e., rea-\nsoning). Specially, we propose an invoking-\nlinearization-generation procedure to support\nLLMs in reasoning on the structured data with\nthe help of the interfaces. By iterating this\nprocedure with provided interfaces, our ap-\nproach can gradually approach the target an-\nswers to a given query. Experiments conducted\non three types of structured data show that\nStructGPT greatly improves the performance\nof LLMs, under the few-shot and zero-shot set-\ntings. Our codes and data are publicly available\nat https://github.com/RUCAIBox/StructGPT.\n1\n",

      "quote": "This maximizes the probability of LLMs generating correct answers based on the retrieved reasoning\npaths.\nThe final objective function of RoG is the combination of the planning optimization and retrieval-\nreasoning optimization, which can be formulated as\nL = log Pθ(a|q, Z∗\nK, G)\n|\n{z\n}\nRetrieval-reasoning\n+\n1\n|Z∗|\nX\nz∈Z∗\nlog Pθ(z|q)\n|\n{z\n}\nPlanning\n.\n(7)\nFrom equation 7, we can see that we adopt the same LLM for both planning and reasoning, which\nare jointly trained on two instruction-tuning tasks, i.e., (planning and retrieval-reasoning). We will\ndiscuss the implementation details of these two tasks in the following subsections.\n4.3\nPLANNING MODULE\nThe planning module aims to generate faithful relation paths as plans for answering the question. To\nutilize the instruction-following ability of LLMs (Wei et al., 2021), we design a simple instruction\ntemplate that prompts LLMs to generate relation paths:\nPlease generate a valid relation path that can be helpful for answering the following question:\n<Question>\nwhere <Question> indicates the question q. The question together with the instruction template\nis fed into LLMs to generate the relation paths, which are structurally formatted as a sentence:\n2The FiD framework assumes each z ∈Z contributes independently, where the probability Pθ(a|q, Z, G)\ncan be approximated as the product of each Pθ(a|q, z, G).\n5\n\nPublished as a conference paper at ICLR 2024\n",

      "quote": "We construct KGs with varying densities by varying the\nhyperparameters of TF-IDF/KNN-ST/KNN-MDR/TAGME,\nand studying its impact on the performance and the neighbor\nmatching time of MD-QA using KGP-T5. Since the LLM-\nbased graph traversal agent selects the next node to visit\nfrom neighbors of already visited nodes, the chance that it\nhits the supporting facts increases as neighbors increase. In\ncontrast, the neighbor matching efficiency decreases as the\ncandidate pool, i.e., Nj in Eq (1), increases. As evidenced\nin Figure 6, we observe a similar trend, i.e., as KG density\nincreases, the F1/EM increases and stays stable while the\nlatency for selecting the most promising neighbors to visit\nnext also increases. KNN-MDR achieves better performance\nthan KNN-ST when the density of the two constructed KGs\nis the same. This is because the encoder in KNN-ST is\npre-trained on wide-spectrum datasets while the encoder in\nMDR is specifically pre-trained on the HotpotQA by the pre-\ntext task of predicting the next supporting facts. Therefore,\nthe embedding similarity and the corresponding neighbor re-\nlations better reflect the logical associations among differ-\nent passages, which aligns with the better constructed KG\nby KNN-MDR than KG by KNN-ST in Figure 5.       "quote": "Introduction\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have demon-\nstrated remarkable success in open-domain ques-\ntion answering. However, they continue to face\nchallenges such as hallucinations and knowledge\ncutoffs (Ji et al., 2023a,b; Yao et al., 2023; Xu et al.,\n2024; Wei et al., 2024). To address these issues,\nrecent research has explored in-context learning\nwith LLM, using external knowledge sources such\nas retrieved documents or knowledge graphs (KG)\nto improve their accuracy and reasoning ability\n(Hogan et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2024; Agrawal et al.,\n2024; Shen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Rosset\net al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2020a;\nZhu et al., 2023a). Among the popular approaches\nare RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) and KAPING (Baek\net al., 2023), which provide context by retrieving\nrelevant documents or KG triplets to support the\nLLM reasoning process. Although these methods\nhave proven effective, few approaches have fully\nintegrated LLMs into the retrieval process, leav-\ning a gap in the ability to efficiently navigate and\nextract relevant information from vast knowledge\nsources.\nRecently, Wang et al. (2023) propose Knowl-\nedge Graph Prompting (KGP), which incorporates\na fine-tuned LLM agent into the KG traversal pro-\ncess. This agent predicts missing evidence based on\nthe initial query and the retrieved documents. The\npredictions are then used to identify relevant pas-\nsages from neighboring nodes in the KG through\nsimilarity ranking. With this prompt reformulation\napproach, KGP achieves state-of-the-art results in\nseveral benchmarks for factual consistency.\n",

      "quote": "We construct KGs with varying densities by varying the\nhyperparameters of TF-IDF/KNN-ST/KNN-MDR/TAGME,\nand studying its impact on the performance and the neighbor\nmatching time of MD-QA using KGP-T5. Since the LLM-\nbased graph traversal agent selects the next node to visit\nfrom neighbors of already visited nodes, the chance that it\nhits the supporting facts increases as neighbors increase. In\ncontrast, the neighbor matching efficiency decreases as the\ncandidate pool, i.e., Nj in Eq (1), increases. As evidenced\nin Figure 6, we observe a similar trend, i.e., as KG density\nincreases, the F1/EM increases and stays stable while the\nlatency for selecting the most promising neighbors to visit\nnext also increases. KNN-MDR achieves better performance\nthan KNN-ST when the density of the two constructed KGs\nis the same. This is because the encoder in KNN-ST is\npre-trained on wide-spectrum datasets while the encoder in\nMDR is specifically pre-trained on the HotpotQA by the pre-\ntext task of predicting the next supporting facts. Therefore,\nthe embedding similarity and the corresponding neighbor re-\nlations better reflect the logical associations among differ-\nent passages, which aligns with the better constructed KG\nby KNN-MDR than KG by KNN-ST in Figure 5.       "quote": "Table 2: Follow-upQA examples of input questions, given information, and the corresponding follow-up questions\ngenerated.\nencoding passages and connecting them based on\ncosine similarity.\n2.3\nCurious LLM Traversal Agent\nWe introduce CuriousLLM as our graph traversal\nagent to enhance the KGP framework. This ap-\nproach is rooted in intuitive reasoning. For ex-\nample, when asked to determine who is older, Bob\nBryan or Mariaan de Swardt, and given information\nabout Bob’s age, one would intuitively ask a follow-\nup question about Mariaan’s age. This follow-up\nquestion guides the search for relevant informa-\ntion. This intuition forms the basis of Follow-upQA\nand our model’s training objective. The advan-\ntage of this approach is that, although the passages\nabout Bob’s and Mariaan’s ages are unrelated, or,\nin other words, not semantically similar, the follow-\nup question about Mariaan’s age creates a logical\nlink between them. As a result, instead of matching\ntwo unrelated passages, once we find one passage,\nwe can identify the other through follow-up ques-\ntions. Furthermore, we train the LLM agent to\nknow when to end the search, and this early termi-\nnation mechanism significantly reduces the latency\nassociated with the original T5 agent.\n",

      "quote": "The integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) with\nlarge language models (LLMs), particularly in med-\nical contexts, presents several potential challenges.\nOne significant concern is the risk of replicating\nany existing biases or errors in the knowledge\ngraphs.       "quote": "To generate a mind map and find final results, we\nprovide LLMs with a prompt that has five compo-\nnents: a system instruction, a question, evidence\ngraphs Gm, a graph-of-thought instruction, and ex-\nemplars.       "quote": "Abstract\nLarge Language Models (LLMs) have achieved\nsignificant success in open-domain question an-\nswering. However, they continue to face chal-\nlenges such as hallucinations and knowledge\ncutoffs. These issues can be mitigated through\nin-context learning by providing LLMs with\nrelevant context before generating answers.\nRecent literature proposes Knowledge Graph\nPrompting (KGP) which integrates knowledge\ngraphs with an LLM-based traversal agent\nto substantially enhance document retrieval\nquality. However, KGP requires costly fine-\ntuning with large datasets and remains prone\nto hallucination. In this paper, we propose\nCuriousLLM, an enhancement that integrates\na curiosity-driven reasoning mechanism into\nan LLM agent. This mechanism enables the\nagent to generate relevant follow-up questions,\nthereby guiding the information retrieval pro-\ncess more efficiently. Central to our approach\nis the development of the new Follow-upQA\ndataset, which includes questions and support-\ning evidence as input, with follow-up ques-\ntions serving as ground truths. These follow-\nup questions either inquire about what is still\nmissing to fully answer the user’s query or\nuse special tokens to signify that the retrieved\nevidence is sufficient. Our experiments show\nthat CuriousLLM significantly boosts LLM per-\nformance in multi-document question answer-\ning (MD-QA), circumventing the substantial\ncomputational costs and latency from the orig-\ninal KGP framework. Source code: https:\n//github.com/zukangy/KGP-CuriousLLM.\n1\n",

      "quote": "The integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) with\nlarge language models (LLMs), particularly in med-\nical contexts, presents several potential challenges.\nOne significant concern is the risk of replicating\nany existing biases or errors in the knowledge\ngraphs. These graphs, often built from pre-existing\ndata sources, might contain outdated or partial in-\nformation, which could inadvertently influence the\nLLM’s outputs. Another issue lies in the integra-\ntion complexity between KGs and LLMs, which\ncould lead to unexpected errors or logical incon-\nsistencies, especially when addressing intricate or\nvague queries. This aspect is critically important\nin the medical field, where precision is paramount.\nMoreover, there’s a possibility that the LLMs might\nbecome excessively dependent on the KGs, which\ncould hinder their performance in scenarios where\nKGs are not accessible or are lacking in infor-\nmation. Additionally, the use of \"mind maps\" to\ntrace the LLMs’ reasoning paths, while innovative,\nraises questions about the models’ interpretability.\nIf these visual representations are complex or ob-\nscure, it may be difficult for users to understand\nhow conclusions were reached, potentially dimin-\nishing trust in these advanced systems. In summary,\nwhile the merger of KGs with LLMs is a promising\ndevelopment, it is crucial to address these poten-\ntial issues to ensure the responsible and efficacious\napplication of this technology.\n\n(b)\nReference\n(c)\nOutput \nMindMap\nGPT-3.5\n(a)\nQuestion\n",

      "quote": "Table 2: Follow-upQA examples of input questions, given information, and the corresponding follow-up questions\ngenerated.\nencoding passages and connecting them based on\ncosine similarity.\n2.3\nCurious LLM Traversal Agent\nWe introduce CuriousLLM as our graph traversal\nagent to enhance the KGP framework. This ap-\nproach is rooted in intuitive reasoning. For ex-\nample, when asked to determine who is older, Bob\nBryan or Mariaan de Swardt, and given information\nabout Bob’s age, one would intuitively ask a follow-\nup question about Mariaan’s age. This follow-up\nquestion guides the search for relevant informa-\ntion. This intuition forms the basis of Follow-upQA\nand our model’s training objective. The advan-\ntage of this approach is that, although the passages\nabout Bob’s and Mariaan’s ages are unrelated, or,\nin other words, not semantically similar, the follow-\nup question about Mariaan’s age creates a logical\nlink between them. As a result, instead of matching\ntwo unrelated passages, once we find one passage,\nwe can identify the other through follow-up ques-\ntions. Furthermore, we train the LLM agent to\nknow when to end the search, and this early termi-\nnation mechanism significantly reduces the latency\nassociated with the original T5 agent.\n",

      "quote": "i\n, c(h)\nj )}, where c(k)\ni\nand c(h)\nj\ndenote the i-th and j-th columns in the\nk-th and h-th tables, respectively.\nProblem Statement. This work mainly focuses\non using LLMs to solve complex reasoning tasks\nbased on structured data. Formally, it can be de-\nscribed as a question answering task: given a nat-\nural language question q and an accessible struc-\ntured data S (e.g., a knowledge graph, a table, or\ndatabase), the LLM needs to extract useful evi-\ndence from S and then generates the expected re-\nsult to answer the question q based on the extracted\nevidence. According to the task requirement, the\ngenerated result can be either free-form answers\nin natural language or structured expressions (e.g.,\nSQL statements) to be executed for obtaining the\nanswer from S. Since we consider three types of\nstructured data (Section 4), our tasks can be instan-\ntiated as follows:\n• KG based question answering (KGQA)\n• Table based question answering (TableQA)\n• DB based semantic parsing (Text-to-SQL)\n4\nApproach\n4.1\nOverview\n",

      "quote": "• LLM Rerankers: Claude3 and GPT-4 rerankers [11, 62]. These models improve the precision of\ntop-k ada-002 results by reranking them using large language models. We employ GPT-4-turbo\n(gpt-4-1106-preview) and Claude3 (claude-3-opus), setting k = 20 for synthesized\nqueries and k = 10 for human-generated queries. Given a query, the LLMs assign a satisfaction\nscore from 0 to 1 to each candidate entity based on textual and relational information. Due to high\ncomputational costs, we evaluate these rerankers on a random 10% sample of test queries.\nThe performance of these models are measured using standard retrieval metrics below.\n• Hit@k assesses whether the correct item is among the top-k results from the model. We used\nk = 1 and k = 5 for evaluation. At k = 1, it evaluates the accuracy of the top recommendation; at\nk = 5, it examines the model’s precision in a wider recommendation set.\n• Recall@k measures the proportion of relevant items in the top-k results. For synthesized queries,\nk = 20 is used, as the answer length of all of the queries in our benchmarks are equal or smaller\nthen 20. This metric offers insight into the model’s ability to identify all relevant items, particularly\nin scenarios where missing any could be critical.\n",

      "quote": "Experiment\nWe conduct experiments on three complex rea-\nsoning tasks over structured data, i.e., KGQA,\nTableQA, and DB based text-to-SQL.\n5.1\nDatasets\nFor KG based QA (KGQA), we adopt two\nbenchmark datasets, i.e., WebQuestionsSP (We-\nbQSP) (Yih et al., 2016) and MetaQA (Zhang et al.,\n2018) for evaluation. The answer entities in We-\nbQSP require up to 2-hop reasoning on the Free-\nbase KG. In contrast, MetaQA contains questions\nin the movie domain, whose answer entities are up\nto 3 hops away from the topic entities on a movie\nKG (based on OMDb). According to the num-\nber of hops, it is split into three sub-datasets, i.e.,\nMetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop.\nFor Table based QA (TableQA), we adopt\nthree widely-used datasets, weakly-supervised Wik-\niSQL (WikiSQL) (Zhong et al., 2017), WikiTable-\nQuestions (WTQ) (Pasupat and Liang, 2015), and\nTabFact (Chen et al., 2020). The first two are typ-\nical table-based question answering datasets, and\nthe third one is a multiple-choice dataset that con-\ncentrates on table fact verification. WikiSQL re-\nquires filtering and aggregating information over\nthe table content, and the WTQ demands more\nadvanced reasoning capabilities (e.g., sorting). Tab-\nFact needs to judge whether the provided statement\nagrees with the facts stored in a table.\n",

      "quote": "To our knowledge, this is the first work that ex-\nplores how to support LLMs in reasoning on multi-\nple types of structured data (including tables, KGs,\nand DBs) in a unified paradigm. To evaluate the ef-\nfectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive\nexperiments on a wide range of tasks (e.g., KG-\nbased question answering (KGQA), Table-based\nquestion answering (TableQA), and DB-based Text-\nto-SQL). Experimental results on 8 datasets demon-\nstrate that our approach can effectively enhance the\nreasoning performance of LLMs on structured data\nin zero-shot and few-shot settings, even compara-\nble with competitive full-data supervised-tuning\nmethods. For example, in KGQA, TableQA, and\nText-to-SQL tasks, our approach yields an increase\nof 11.4% of Hits@1 on WebQSP, 4.2% of accu-\nracy in TabFact, and 4.7% of execution accuracy\nin Spider respectively, compared to directly using\nChatGPT in the zero-shot setting.\n2\n",

      "quote": "i\n, c(h)\nj )}, where c(k)\ni\nand c(h)\nj\ndenote the i-th and j-th columns in the\nk-th and h-th tables, respectively.\nProblem Statement. This work mainly focuses\non using LLMs to solve complex reasoning tasks\nbased on structured data. Formally, it can be de-\nscribed as a question answering task: given a nat-\nural language question q and an accessible struc-\ntured data S (e.g., a knowledge graph, a table, or\ndatabase), the LLM needs to extract useful evi-\ndence from S and then generates the expected re-\nsult to answer the question q based on the extracted\nevidence. According to the task requirement, the\ngenerated result can be either free-form answers\nin natural language or structured expressions (e.g.,\nSQL statements) to be executed for obtaining the\nanswer from S.       "quote": "To our knowledge, this is the first work that ex-\nplores how to support LLMs in reasoning on multi-\nple types of structured data (including tables, KGs,\nand DBs) in a unified paradigm. To evaluate the ef-\nfectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive\nexperiments on a wide range of tasks (e.g., KG-\nbased question answering (KGQA), Table-based\nquestion answering (TableQA), and DB-based Text-\nto-SQL). Experimental results on 8 datasets demon-\nstrate that our approach can effectively enhance the\nreasoning performance of LLMs on structured data\nin zero-shot and few-shot settings, even compara-\nble with competitive full-data supervised-tuning\nmethods. For example, in KGQA, TableQA, and\nText-to-SQL tasks, our approach yields an increase\nof 11.4% of Hits@1 on WebQSP, 4.2% of accu-\nracy in TabFact, and 4.7% of execution accuracy\nin Spider respectively, compared to directly using\nChatGPT in the zero-shot setting.\n2\n",

      "quote": "• LLM Rerankers: Claude3 and GPT-4 rerankers [11, 62]. These models improve the precision of\ntop-k ada-002 results by reranking them using large language models. We employ GPT-4-turbo\n(gpt-4-1106-preview) and Claude3 (claude-3-opus), setting k = 20 for synthesized\nqueries and k = 10 for human-generated queries. Given a query, the LLMs assign a satisfaction\nscore from 0 to 1 to each candidate entity based on textual and relational information. Due to high\ncomputational costs, we evaluate these rerankers on a random 10% sample of test queries.\nThe performance of these models are measured using standard retrieval metrics below.\n• Hit@k assesses whether the correct item is among the top-k results from the model. We used\nk = 1 and k = 5 for evaluation. At k = 1, it evaluates the accuracy of the top recommendation; at\nk = 5, it examines the model’s precision in a wider recommendation set.\n• Recall@k measures the proportion of relevant items in the top-k results. For synthesized queries,\nk = 20 is used, as the answer length of all of the queries in our benchmarks are equal or smaller\nthen 20. This metric offers insight into the model’s ability to identify all relevant items, particularly\nin scenarios where missing any could be critical.\n",

      "quote": "Experiment\nWe conduct experiments on three complex rea-\nsoning tasks over structured data, i.e., KGQA,\nTableQA, and DB based text-to-SQL.\n5.1\nDatasets\nFor KG based QA (KGQA), we adopt two\nbenchmark datasets, i.e., WebQuestionsSP (We-\nbQSP) (Yih et al., 2016) and MetaQA (Zhang et al.,\n2018) for evaluation. The answer entities in We-\nbQSP require up to 2-hop reasoning on the Free-\nbase KG. In contrast, MetaQA contains questions\nin the movie domain, whose answer entities are up\nto 3 hops away from the topic entities on a movie\nKG (based on OMDb). According to the num-\nber of hops, it is split into three sub-datasets, i.e.,\nMetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop, and MetaQA-3hop.\nFor Table based QA (TableQA), we adopt\nthree widely-used datasets, weakly-supervised Wik-\niSQL (WikiSQL) (Zhong et al., 2017), WikiTable-\nQuestions (WTQ) (Pasupat and Liang, 2015), and\nTabFact (Chen et al., 2020). The first two are typ-\nical table-based question answering datasets, and\nthe third one is a multiple-choice dataset that con-\ncentrates on table fact verification. WikiSQL re-\nquires filtering and aggregating information over\nthe table content, and the WTQ demands more\nadvanced reasoning capabilities (e.g., sorting). Tab-\nFact needs to judge whether the provided statement\nagrees with the facts stored in a table.\n",

      "quote": "To our knowledge, this is the first work that ex-\nplores how to support LLMs in reasoning on multi-\nple types of structured data (including tables, KGs,\nand DBs) in a unified paradigm. To evaluate the ef-\nfectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive\nexperiments on a wide range of tasks (e.g., KG-\nbased question answering (KGQA), Table-based\nquestion answering (TableQA), and DB-based Text-\nto-SQL). Experimental results on 8 datasets demon-\nstrate that our approach can effectively enhance the\nreasoning performance of LLMs on structured data\nin zero-shot and few-shot settings, even compara-\nble with competitive full-data supervised-tuning\nmethods. For example, in KGQA, TableQA, and\nText-to-SQL tasks, our approach yields an increase\nof 11.4% of Hits@1 on WebQSP, 4.2% of accu-\nracy in TabFact, and 4.7% of execution accuracy\nin Spider respectively, compared to directly using\nChatGPT in the zero-shot setting.\n2\n",

      "quote": "Abstract\nGiven a graph with textual attributes, we enable users to ‘chat with their graph’:\nthat is, to ask questions about the graph using a conversational interface. In re-\nsponse to a user’s questions, our method provides textual replies and highlights the\nrelevant parts of the graph. While existing works integrate large language models\n(LLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) in various ways, they mostly focus\non either conventional graph tasks (such as node, edge, and graph classification),\nor on answering simple graph queries on small or synthetic graphs. In contrast,\nwe develop a flexible question-answering framework targeting real-world textual\ngraphs, applicable to multiple applications including scene graph understanding,\ncommon sense reasoning, and knowledge graph reasoning. Toward this goal, we\nfirst develop a Graph Question Answering (GraphQA) benchmark with data col-\nlected from different tasks. Then, we propose our G-Retriever method, introducing\nthe first retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach for general textual graphs,\nwhich can be fine-tuned to enhance graph understanding via soft prompting. To\nresist hallucination and to allow for textual graphs that greatly exceed the LLM’s\ncontext window size, G-Retriever performs RAG over a graph by formulating this\ntask as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization problem. Empirical evaluations\nshow that our method outperforms baselines on textual graph tasks from multiple\ndomains, scales well with larger graph sizes, and mitigates hallucination. 1\n1\n",

      "quote": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n",

      "quote": "Figure 3: Overview of the proposed G-Retriever: 1) Indexing: Graphs are indexed for efficient query\nprocessing; 2) Retrieval: The most semantically relevant nodes and edges are retrieved, conditioned\non the query; 3) Subgraph Construction: A connected subgraph is extracted, covering as many\nrelevant nodes and edges as possible while maintaining a manageable graph size; 4) Generation: An\nanswer is generated using a ‘graph prompt’, a textualized graph, and the query.\nrequire multi-hop reasoning. Given the possibility of multiple answers for the same question, the\nhit@1 metric is used to assess the precision of the top returned answer.\n5\nG-Retriever\nIn this section, we introduce G-Retriever, a new architecture tailored for GraphQA, which integrates\nthe strengths of GNNs, LLMs, and RAG. To allow efficient fine-tuning while preserving the LLM’s\npretrained language capabilities, we freeze the LLM and use a soft prompting approach on the output\nof the GNN. Our RAG-based design mitigates hallucinations through direct retrieval of the graph,\nwhile allowing our approach to scale to graphs exceeding the LLM’s context window size. To adapt\nRAG to graphs, we formulate subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization problem. This approach\nalso allows us to enhance explainability by returning the retrieved subgraph.\nG-Retriever comprises four main steps: indexing, retrieval, subgraph construction and generation, as\ndepicted in Figure 3. The implementation details of each step are elaborated in the following sections.\n5.1\nIndexing\n",

      "quote": "PPR Alternatives. As shown in Table 5 (rows 5-6), to examine how much of our results are due to\nthe strength of PPR, we replace the PPR output with the query node probability #»n multiplied by node\nspecificity values (row 5) and a version of this that also distributes a small amount of probability to the\ndirect neighbors of each query node (row 6). First, we find that PPR is a much more effective method\nfor including associations for retrieval on all three datasets compared to both simple baselines. It is\ninteresting to note that adding the neighborhood of Rq nodes without PPR leads to worse performance\nthan only using the query nodes themselves.\nAblations. As seen in Table 5 (rows 7-8), node specificity obtains considerable improvements on\nMuSiQue and HotpotQA and yields almost no change in 2WikiMultiHopQA. This is likely because\n2WikiMultiHopQA relies on named entities with little differences in terms of term weighting. In\ncontrast, synonymy edges have the largest effect on 2WikiMultiHopQA, suggesting that noisy entity\nstandardization is useful when most relevant concepts are named entities, and improvements to\nsynonymy detection could lead to stronger performance in other datasets.\n5.2\nHippoRAG’s Advantage: Single-Step Multi-Hop Retrieval\n",
